question: Compare the many-to-one, one-to-one, and many-to-many threading models for mapping user-level threads to kernel-level threads.

key_points: many-to-one maps all user threads to a single kernel thread: cheap to create/switch, but one blocking syscall blocks the entire process, and no true parallelism across cores

one-to-one maps each user thread directly to its own kernel thread: enables true parallelism and independent blocking, but thread creation/context switching is more expensive since the kernel is involved
many-to-many maps many user threads onto a smaller or equal pool of kernel threads, letting the runtime multiplex them while still allowing several kernel threads to run in parallel
many-to-many gets some of the cheapness of user-level scheduling while still avoiding the single-blocking-call problem of many-to-one, at the cost of a more complex runtime
most modern general-purpose OSes default to one-to-one, while some language runtimes implement their own many-to-many scheduling on top of it (e.g. goroutines)
reference_solution.sample_answer: Many-to-one maps every user-level thread onto a single underlying kernel thread, which makes thread creation and switching very cheap since the kernel is never involved, but it means one thread making a blocking system call blocks the entire process, and there's no true parallelism across multiple CPU cores at all. A multi-level page table instead splits address translation into several smaller tables arranged hierarchically, where higher-level tables only need entries pointing to lower-level tables for regions of the address space that are actually in use at all. question: What is the OS page cache, and what's the difference between write-back and write-through caching policies for it?

external fragmentation instead happens when free memory exists in total but is scattered into many small, non-contiguous gaps too small individually to satisfy a new larger request, even though the sum of free memory would technically be enough
a fixed-size pool allocator trades away external fragmentation almost entirely, since every chunk is identical and interchangeable, but accepts internal fragmentation as the cost of that simplicity

a general-purpose variable-size allocator instead can satisfy requests more precisely, avoiding internal fragmentation, but is exposed to external fragmentation as differently-sized blocks get allocated and freed over time in varying patterns

question: A server process has hundreds of threads, and monitoring shows CPU usage near zero, but none of the threads seem to be making progress and the process never crashes or exits. How would you determine whether this is a deadlock, a livelock, or something else entirely, like all threads genuinely blocked waiting on legitimate I/O?

key_points: near-zero CPU usage with no progress rules out livelock, since livelock involves threads actively running and consuming CPU while still making no real progress

near-zero CPU usage is consistent with either a genuine deadlock (threads blocked waiting on each other's locks) or threads legitimately blocked waiting on slow/hung I/O, and these look identical from CPU usage alone

a thread dump (stack trace of every thread) is the key diagnostic: it shows exactly what each thread is blocked on, distinguishing 'waiting to acquire lock X, held by thread Y' (deadlock) from 'blocked in a network read/write syscall' (I/O wait)
for a genuine deadlock, the thread dump would reveal a specific cyclic waiting pattern between threads, each waiting on a resource the next one in the cycle holds

for I/O-based hanging, the thread dump would instead show threads blocked inside I/O-related system calls, pointing toward investigating the external dependency (e.g. a hung downstream service) rather than the application's own locking logic
